conversation.content:
Hi there, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes I’d like to complete the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short—with you. It’s a brief, 10-question screen that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived. Everything you share is confidential, and my only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported. We’ll just chat through each question; there are no right or wrong answers. Ready to begin?

Thinking back over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Most days I can still laugh at things—like when my husband makes a silly face or when the baby does those little milk-drunk smiles—but I notice it doesn’t come as easily or feel quite as good as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most of the time, yeah—I can still laugh. It’s not every single moment like before, but usually I find myself smiling or chuckling at something goofy my husband does or when the baby makes those funny faces.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes… I still get excited if we’re planning a coffee outing or if my favorite show drops a new episode, but it feels kind of muted. Like, I’ll think “Oh, that should be fun,” yet the buzz doesn’t last; I’m mostly focused on what could go wrong with the baby or whether I’ll be too tired to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a few times this week. Like, if the baby’s extra fussy, I’ll think maybe I ate something that upset his tummy, or if he won’t nap I assume I’m doing the routine wrong. I know it’s probably not really my fault, but those thoughts still pop in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Now and then—like when he’s sleeping a little longer than usual, my mind jumps to “Is he breathing?” or I’ll suddenly worry his next check-up will find something wrong. I can usually calm myself pretty quick, but those worries still sneak up without warning.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky… maybe just a quick jolt of fear, like if I hear him make a weird grunt in the night, but it passes fast. I haven’t had that overwhelming, can’t-breathe kind of panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

A couple of days, yeah. When the laundry piles up and he won’t settle unless I’m holding him, I feel like I’m drowning a bit. Nothing huge, but I’ll stand in the kitchen and think, “How is everyone else doing this without falling apart?” I still manage, just feels heavier than I expected.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, that hasn’t happened. I’ll sometimes need an extra half-hour to fall asleep because my mind’s ticking through the next day’s feedings, but once I’m out I’m out. I’m not lying there miserable or crying at night.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah, I do feel that way some of the time—like a couple of afternoons this week I just felt kind of heavy and down. It comes and goes, though; it’s not all day, every day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I cried twice this week—once when he wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing him, and again yesterday when I dropped a whole pumped bottle on the floor. It was more the frustration building up than constant misery.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’ve felt tired or overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Identified Symptoms / Concerns  
- Low mood: episodic sadness, “heavy” feeling several afternoons/week  
- Anhedonia: enjoyment present but “muted,” anticipatory worry overrides pleasure  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame for infant’s fussiness or perceived feeding failures  
- Anxiety: unprovoked worries about infant safety, transient nocturnal startle  
- Overwhelm: periodic sense of “drowning,” comparison to others, feels “heavier than expected”  
- Crying spells: twice this week linked to feeding/pumping frustration  
- Sleep: delayed onset only, no middle-insomnia or early-morning wakening

Pattern  
Mild, intermittent depressive and anxiety symptoms begin ~2 weeks postpartum; no daily persistence or functional incapacity; no self-harm ideation.

Screening Significance  
Meets subthreshold criteria for possible minor postpartum depression and/or postpartum anxiety; full criteria for major depressive episode or panic disorder not endorsed at present.

Risk Factors Present  
- Situational tearfulness, guilt, low enjoyment  
- Transient anxious arousal  
- Absence of suicidal ideation (documented)

Plan  
Provide psycho-education, normalize common postpartum mood changes, encourage sleep/support hygiene, schedule follow-up screening in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate, suicidal thoughts develop, or functioning declines.
